name: Willy Brandt
role: German chancellor (1969-1974), SPD chairman (1964-1987), Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1971
summary: Willy Brandt was a democratic socialist who combined a market order with an expanding social state, co-determination and educational reform at home, and a policy of renouncing force, détente and treaties with the East abroad while staying firmly anchored in NATO and West European integration. He rejected communist dictatorship from his 1948 Prague speech onward, favoured pooling sovereignty in a European union, and later chaired the North-South Commission calling for a restructured world economy and more aid.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: 1969 declaration: lasting stability and growth are possible only in a functioning market order, with competition as the surest guarantee of performance; 1987: the commitment to competition and the market principle needs no qualification. regulate-corporations.rationale: 1969: announces preventive merger control across the economy, an independent monopoly commission, tighter abuse control of dominant firms and press merger control, plus consumer protection in food and advertising.

notes: Historical figure (died 1992): answers rest on his own speeches (1948-1989) and his record in office; low answers beginning "Inferred:" are drawn only from stated views. Changed positions: anti-communist hard line in 1948 gave way to coexistence and treaties with the East (1960s-70s); he backed the 1972 Radikalenerlass and later called it a painful mistake (1987). Full text of the 1980 Brandt Report introduction could not be retrieved, so Brandt Commission positions rest on his 1978 speech chairing it. His personal views on nuclear power, drugs, same-sex law and the death penalty were not found in the sources reviewed.
